title: The Shape of Sorry
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 27 of 40
content:
The pasta had turned into a single damp opinion about disappointment.

I'd cooked it because Greg said he'd be home for dinner. I had even put the little battery candles on the table, since I knew we'd both end up knocking over real ones. At eight, the food was cold. At nine, I stopped looking at the clock and started doing the dishes.

At ten, he came through the door with wet flowers and a broken umbrella.

"Okay," he said. "I have a really bad explanation."

"That makes two of us. I have really bad pasta."

He tried to laugh. I couldn't.

Greg lowered the flowers.

He had been helping a neighbor whose van wouldn't start. One repair had become another, then a trip to find the right belt, then a long drive back. The neighbor was safe. Greg had his phone. He just hadn't called because every time he looked up, he thought he'd be done in five more minutes.

"Did you think I wouldn't notice?" I asked.

"No. I thought I could still make it."

"At ten?"

He rubbed his face. "I know."

I didn't want to be cruel. I also didn't want to turn my hurt into a little smile that would teach him there was no cost to letting me wait.

"Can we sit down?" I asked.

He took the chair opposite me. The flowers dripped onto the table. He put them in the sink, then sat again without asking whether that made everything better.

"I was excited about tonight," I said. "Not because you were supposed to prove something. Just because I'd saved the evening for us."

"I was excited too."

"Then why was I the last person you thought to tell?"

He looked at his hands.

"Because that neighbor was right there asking me for help," he said. "You weren't. And I thought if I called, I'd have to say I was choosing something else instead of you."

"Not calling was a choice too."

"Yeah."

The apology came slowly. Not dramatic, not lyrical. He said he'd left me waiting, that I had every reason to be upset, and that he wouldn't make me responsible for reassuring him while he apologized.

I nearly cried at that. I hated how much a plain sentence could matter.

"Are you asking me to forgive you now?" I asked.

"No. I'd like it eventually. But right now I'm trying to listen."

We reheated what was left of the pasta and added a little water until it was at least edible. Greg offered to go out and buy dinner instead. I said no. Buying an expensive meal wasn't the same as showing up.

While the sauce warmed, we made a practical plan. If he accepted a favor that would affect our agreed time, he'd send a message. If he couldn't safely stop to call, he'd tell me as soon as he could. If he needed to cancel, we'd decide whether to reschedule instead of leaving the evening hanging. I promised not to treat every late arrival as a verdict on how much he loved me.

"I have other partners, Greg," I said, not because he had forgotten but because it mattered to the plan. "I've been clear that I'm ethically non-monogamous and prefer polyamory. I keep a calendar because the people I love shouldn't have to guess whether I'm coming. You deserve that from me too."

He nodded. "I don't want to be the guy who makes plans impossible."

"Then start with one plan you can keep."

"Tomorrow breakfast?"

"I have an early visit tomorrow."

He smiled ruefully. "Okay. See, this is why I should have asked."

"Friday evening?"

"Friday. I'll put it in writing."

He took a receipt from his pocket and wrote our agreed time on the back. Then he paused. "Actually, I'll put it somewhere I won't accidentally wash it."

"The bar is rising."

He laughed for real.

The next morning a neighbor came by the car wash asking whether Greg could look at a faulty engine. He said he could inspect it after his booked work, not immediately. The neighbor went elsewhere for the emergency repair. Nobody died of disappointment.

On Friday, Greg arrived on time with a bag of vegetables and a determination not to touch the stove without instructions. The meal was better. We laughed about the first disaster, but we didn't pretend it hadn't hurt.

When dinner was done, he reached across the table.

"Want me to hold your hand?" he asked.

"Yes."

We sat there until I was the one who leaned in for a kiss. It was warm, familiar, and still had a little awkwardness in it. We closed the curtains later, with no audience and no need to perform an apology beyond what we'd actually changed.

The broken umbrella stayed by the door for a week. Then Greg fixed it, tested it in the rain, and gave it back to the neighbor he'd borrowed it from.

I liked that he remembered a promise small enough not to become a song.
